summary: A country in the eastern part of the Caribbean island of Hispaniola; its capital, Santo Domingo, is one of the earliest cities founded by Europeans in the Americas, and the country is known for baseball and merengue music.

ranking.name: Catholicism
ranking.description: Hispaniola was Spain’s first colony in the Americas, and Catholicism arrived with colonization from the 1490s; Santo Domingo has the earliest cathedral and university in the Americas (1538), and in 1511 the Dominican friar Montesinos delivered here his famous sermon condemning the mistreatment of the indigenous people. In 1954 the dictator Trujillo signed a concordat with the Vatican granting Catholicism a special position. The patroness, Our Lady of Altagracia, draws large numbers of pilgrims to Higüey every 21 January, but the proportion of believers has fallen markedly in recent decades.

ranking.name: Protestantism (Evangelical)
ranking.description: During Haitian rule in 1824 a group of free African Americans from the United States settled on the Samaná Peninsula, bringing Methodist and other Protestant churches; during the American military occupation of 1916–1924, American missions further established schools and churches. Since the 1970s Pentecostal and other evangelical churches have expanded rapidly in poor neighborhoods and the countryside, and their share is now close to one-quarter.

ranking.name: No religion
ranking.description: With urbanization, overseas migration and rising education among young people, more and more Dominicans, though retaining a Christian cultural background, no longer identify with a particular denomination, and the non-religious population has grown rapidly in the 21st century, especially in large cities such as Santo Domingo and Santiago.

ranking.name: Other
ranking.description: These include Jehovah’s Witnesses, Mormonism, and Dominican folk beliefs that fuse Catholic saints with African spirits (such as the “Twenty-One Divisions” belief, Vudú Dominicano); the latter have historical ties to Haitian Vodou, but most adherents also consider themselves Catholics, so the proportion in statistics is very low.

religion.background: The Dominican Republic occupies the eastern part of Hispaniola, where Columbus landed in 1492, and is the starting point of Catholicism’s entry into the Americas; the colonial church established here the New World’s earliest dioceses and university. Haitian rule and free African American immigrants in the 19th century brought Protestantism, and the American occupation in the early 20th century further extended Protestant influence. Catholicism enjoyed state support during the Trujillo dictatorship (1930–1961), but the rise of evangelicalism and accelerating secularization in the late 20th century have made the religious structure increasingly diverse.

ranking.name: Spanish
ranking.description: After Columbus arrived in 1492, Spain established the first colonial cities of the Americas on the island, the indigenous Taíno rapidly died out from war and disease, and Spanish became the mainstream language. During the Haitian rule of the whole island from 1822 to 1844, Spanish instead became a marker of identity distinguishing Dominicans from Haitians, and its position became even more secure after independence in 1844. Dominican Spanish clearly swallows consonants, and the accent of the Cibao region in the north is especially distinctive.

ranking.name: Haitian Creole
ranking.description: In the early 20th century, sugar plantations owned by American capital brought in large numbers of Haitian workers, who lived together in cane-worker camps called “bateyes,” and so Haitian Creole persisted in the border area and plantation zones. The “Parsley Massacre” of 1937, in which Trujillo ordered the killing of Haitians on the border, and the 2013 Constitutional Court ruling that stripped the descendants of Haitian immigrants of citizenship have both left the Haitian-descended community in a long-term marginal position.

language.history: The Taíno language vanished along with the indigenous people, leaving only loanwords such as huracán, hamaca (hammock) and canoa, which later even entered English. Spanish has been the main language of the island since the end of the 15th century and has been influenced by the languages of African slaves and the accents of Canary Islands immigrants. Haitian rule in the 19th century and the American occupation in the 20th century (1916–1924) brought, respectively, the influence of a French-based Creole and of English. Today Spanish is the only official language, and Haitian Creole is the largest immigrant language.

ranking.name: La bandera (“the flag”)
ranking.description: A lunch plate made up of white rice, stewed red beans, stewed chicken or beef and a green salad, often with fried plantain as well, with generous portions and balanced nutrition.
ranking.history: The name means “the flag,” because the colors of the white rice, red beans and stewed meat bring to mind the national flag, symbolizing the dish’s national standing in Dominican cuisine. The rice comes from the rice cultivation introduced by Spanish colonists, while the beans and the stewing method blend the food traditions of the indigenous people and African slaves. It is the most typical Dominican midday meal, and almost every household and small restaurant serves it every day.

ranking.name: Mangú (mashed plantain)
ranking.description: Green plantains are boiled and mashed, mixed with butter or oil, and topped with vinegar-pickled sautéed red onions, often served with fried salami, fried cheese and fried eggs.
ranking.history: The plantain was brought to the Caribbean by the Spanish in the 16th century and became a staple of plantation slaves, and the way of mashing it resembles the West African tradition of pounding starchy crops into a paste. Folk tradition says the name came from American soldiers during the 1916–1924 occupation who praised it with “Man, good!”, but scholars think it more likely derives from a word of the African Kongo languages. The combination with fried salami, fried cheese and fried eggs is called “los tres golpes” (the three hits) and is the most classic Dominican breakfast.

ranking.name: Sancocho
ranking.description: Several kinds of meat such as chicken, beef and pork are slow-stewed with root vegetables such as plantain, cassava, yam and corn into a thick stew, served with white rice and avocado.
ranking.history: Sancocho derives from the stews of Spain’s Canary Islands, which in the colonial period combined with the indigenous root crops and African stewing methods to form versions across the Caribbean and Latin America. The most lavish in the Dominican Republic is the “sancocho de siete carnes” (seven-meat sancocho). It is usually simmered in a large pot for family gatherings on festivals, birthdays, New Year or rainy days, and is regarded as one of the Dominican Republic’s national dishes.

ranking.name: Tostones (fried plantain slices)
ranking.description: Green plantains are cut into chunks, fried until soft, flattened and fried again, crisp outside and fluffy inside, sprinkled with salt and served as a side dish or snack, often alongside fried chicken or fried fish.
ranking.history: The plantain is a crop brought to the Caribbean by the Spanish from Africa and the Canary Islands in the 16th century, and the double-frying method spread throughout the Caribbean region; Dominicans also call it “fritos verdes” (fried greens). It is the most common side dish beside la bandera, fried chicken and fried fish, and also a signature of beach snack stalls, reflecting the blending of African and Spanish food cultures.

ranking.name: Habichuelas con dulce (sweet bean cream)
ranking.description: Red beans are cooked until soft and strained into a thick bean cream, to which coconut milk, condensed milk, sweet potato, raisins, cinnamon and clove are added; it can be eaten hot or cold, often with small cookies.
ranking.history: Habichuelas con dulce is a dessert unique to the Dominican Republic, inseparable from the Catholic traditions of Lent and Holy Week: during the meatless Lenten period, households cook large quantities and share them with neighbors and relatives, forming a communal custom of sharing. It combines the beans of the Americas, the coconut of the Caribbean and spices imported through colonial trade, and is regarded as part of Dominican food identity.
